channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Your choices often follow the crowd's momentum.
item.description: The probability of an individual adopting a behavior increases as more people do the same, because individuals use others' actions as signals of information to make more accurate decisions.

item.title: You are less likely to help if others are watching.
item.description: The presence of other witnesses significantly reduces the individual probability that someone will offer help in an emergency.

item.title: You judge a person's character by their appearance.
item.description: The 'halo effect' was identified by Thorndike in 1920, but the specific 'what is beautiful is good' stereotype regarding intelligence and kindness is most famously attributed to a 1972 study.

item.title: You react differently to the same information framed differently.
item.description: The framing effect, where choice is influenced by whether information is presented as gains or losses, was famously explored by Tversky and Kahneman in 1981 using the 'Asian disease' scenario (600 lives) rather than a 90%/10% percentage model.

item.title: You can be nudged by an irrelevant third option.
item.description: Consumers are more likely to pick a higher-priced item when a slightly worse version is presented as a decoy.

item.title: You rewrite your history to suit your present.
item.description: After learning an outcome, you shift your past confidence to make the result seem inevitable.

item.title: You cannot un-know what you have already learned.
item.description: Once you acquire knowledge, you systematically overestimate how easily others can grasp the same concept.

item.title: You scan the world for what you expect.
item.description: A 1979 study found that people perceive ambiguous evidence as supporting their existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory data.

item.title: You accept arguments based on the speaker's rank.
item.description: A 1974 study found that people are significantly more likely to comply with requests if they believe the person holds authority.

item.title: You ignore the numbers when a story is better.
item.description: A 1973 study showed that people ignore objective probability when presented with a specific, compelling description.

item.title: You think that thing matters more than it does.
item.description: A 1998 study found that people overestimate how much a single change, like moving to California, impacts their long-term happiness.

item.title: You decide based on feelings, then justify with logic.
item.description: A 2000 study by Finucane, Alhakami, Slovic, and Johnson demonstrated that people evaluate the risks and benefits of an activity based on their affective associations.

item.title: You believe your own opinions are the default setting.
item.description: Research shows that people consistently overestimate the proportion of the population that shares their specific preferences.

item.title: You take credit for your wins and blame bad luck elsewhere.
item.description: The self-serving bias is the tendency to perceive oneself as responsible for successes and external factors as responsible for failures, though researchers like Miller and Ross (1975) argued this may stem from information processing rather than ego defense.

item.title: You assume a physically attractive person is also inherently virtuous.
item.description: Thorndike's original 1920 study observed that military officers tended to rate their subordinates' specific traits (like leadership or intelligence) as consistently high or low based on a general impression, rather than independent evaluation.

item.title: You assume you influence things that are purely random.
item.description: People are more confident in their ability to win a game of chance if they feel a sense of personal involvement.

item.title: You are not being watched as much as you think.
item.description: A 2000 study showed that people vastly overestimate how much others notice their appearance or actions in public.

item.title: The first number you hear dictates your entire decision.
item.description: People estimating the value of an item are consistently pulled toward the first number they are given, even if it is irrelevant.

item.title: You assume everyone sees the world exactly like you.
item.description: Most people believe their subjective interpretation of events is an objective reflection of reality.

item.title: You learn significantly more by forgetting a little bit.
item.description: Distributed learning sessions result in longer retention than cramming the same amount of time into one sitting.

item.title: You look more attractive when surrounded by other people.
item.description: A 2013 study found that faces are rated as more attractive in a group than when shown individually.

item.title: You assume your memories are accurate replays of reality.
item.description: Human memory is a reconstructive process where, under certain conditions, a retrieved memory can enter a labile state and undergo reconsolidation, making it susceptible to modification.

item.title: You value things more just because you helped build them.
item.description: The effort you invest in a project creates an irrational attachment to the final result.

item.title: You miss what is right in front of you.
item.description: In the 1999 Simons and Chabris study, approximately 46% of observers failed to notice an opaque gorilla, though this percentage varied by experimental condition.

item.title: You think media influences others, but not you.
item.description: People consistently perceive mass media as having a greater effect on others than on themselves.

item.title: Being perfect makes you less likable, not more.
item.description: A competent person becomes more attractive and relatable when they commit a minor, clumsy error.

item.title: You exaggerate the impact of any single factor.
item.description: Humans systematically overestimate the importance of whatever they are currently focusing on, like a new car or a job.

item.title: You evaluate objects differently based on what you saw before.
item.description: The contrast effect suggests that human judgment is relative; we assess items based on the ones perceived immediately prior.

item.title: You believe you are safer from misfortune than everyone else.
item.description: The optimism bias leads people to underestimate their personal risk of experiencing negative events like divorce or illness.

item.title: You remember experiences based only on the ending, not duration.
item.description: In a 1993 study, participants rated an uncomfortable experience more favorably if the end was less painful, regardless of total time.

item.title: You value an object more once it becomes yours.
item.description: The endowment effect shows that ownership increases your valuation of an item, even if you acquired it moments ago.

item.title: You are more likely to agree after you have refused.
item.description: The door-in-the-face technique uses the psychological pressure of concession to secure a smaller request.

item.title: You see patterns where none actually exist.
item.description: Illusory correlation causes you to perceive a relationship between two variables even when they are statistically unrelated.

item.title: A rhyme makes a statement seem more truthful to you.
item.description: The rhyme-as-reason effect increases the perceived accuracy of a statement simply because it is phonologically pleasing.

item.title: You think the past forces a change in probability.
item.description: A 1971 study found that people expect a coin flip to balance out after a streak of heads, as if the coin has a memory.

item.title: You will invent reasons for a choice you never made.
item.description: In a 2005 experiment, participants provided confabulated explanations in approximately 82% of the trials where they failed to notice that the face they were justifying was not the one they had chosen.

item.title: You cling to your convictions even when proven false.
item.description: A 1975 study found that participants still believed in their own ability to detect suicide notes even after researchers told them their previous feedback was fabricated.

item.title: You determine the truth by how quickly it arrives.
item.description: A 1991 study found that people who were asked to recall six instances of assertive behavior rated themselves as more assertive than those asked to recall twelve.

item.title: You cannot imagine not knowing what you already know.
item.description: A 1990 experiment showed that people assume listeners will identify a tapped song 50% of the time, while the actual rate is only 2.5%.

item.title: You are convinced past events were easier to predict.
item.description: In a 1975 study, participants rated an outcome as significantly more inevitable once they were told it had already happened.

item.title: You define your worth by measuring it against others.
item.description: A 1954 study proposed that in the absence of objective standards, humans evaluate their abilities through social comparison.

item.title: You carry unconscious biases that contradict your explicit values.
item.description: A 1998 study found that participants were slower to associate positive words with non-white faces, even when they stated no conscious bias.

item.title: You cannot imagine what it is like not knowing.
item.description: A 1990 study found that people who knew a song's rhythm consistently overestimated how many people would recognize it by tapping.

item.title: You claim personal credit for wins but blame luck.
item.description: A 1978 study showed that participants took credit for success but attributed failure to external variables like test difficulty.

item.title: You see your group as diverse but others uniform.
item.description: A 1980 study by Quattrone and Jones titled 'The Perception of Variability Within and Across Groups' found that individuals perceive out-groups as more homogeneous than in-groups.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes immediate comfort over future success.
item.description: A 1981 study found that pigeons consistently prefer a small reward now over a larger one in the future.

item.title: You believe your perception is the objective truth.
item.description: A 1996 study showed that people assume their perspective is rational, while disagreement implies others are biased or uninformed.

item.title: You overestimate how much people read your internal state.
item.description: A 1998 study found that people significantly overestimate their ability to hide their true emotions from observers.

item.title: A random number changes how you value a price.
item.description: A 1974 study found that people estimated the percentage of African nations in the UN differently depending on a random number spun on a wheel.

item.title: You exert less effort when you work in a group.
item.description: The term 'social loafing' was coined and established by Latané, Williams, and Harkins in 1979.
